verses.translation_literal: Of David. YHWH [is] my light and my salvation: of whom shall I be afraid? YHWH [is] the stronghold of my life: of whom shall I be in dread?
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is my light, and my rescue. Of whom, then, should I be afraid? The LORD is the fortress round my very life. Before whom should I tremble?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a declaration in the dark, not a boast in daylight. Light and salvation travel together here: Radak says trouble is like darkness and deliverance is the dawn, and Ibn Ezra hears 'light' as the night-time cure for a frightened soul. Play the two questions as a man listing his reasons for fear and finding each one empty. They are real questions, not rhetorical flourishes: the singer is deciding, line by line, not to be afraid.

The KJV 'strength of my life' flattens a concrete word. מָעוֹז is a fortified refuge, a place you retreat into and shut the gate behind; Radak sets it beside a tower. The KJV also puts 'A Psalm of David' before the verse; the Hebrew has only a lamed, 'of / for David', which may mean author, dedicatee or collection, and the KJV decided. Hebrew also uses two different verbs for fear: יָרֵא ('I shall fear', the known threat) and פָּחַד ('I shall be in dread', the hidden one). Malbim makes the distinction: visible enemies versus ones who plot in secret. English 'afraid' twice loses that step from fear to dread.

philological_notes.note: 'My light': the divine name is predicated with a bare noun, 'YHWH [is] my light'. The image is of safe sight at night and of deliverance after a dark time; it is not a sun-god title, in a world where Shamash, the sun, was the god of justice and rescue.

A stronghold or place of refuge, from the root for strength. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'strength' (חוזק), so the abstract sense is attested, but the next word, 'of my life', makes the fortress picture natural.
Two verbs for fear in a parallel pair. Malbim reads the first as fear of a known threat, the second as dread of the unknown; that reading is his, the Hebrew may simply be poetic variation.

verses.translation_literal: When evildoers drew near against me to eat my flesh, my adversaries and my enemies, [they] against me, they stumbled and fell.
verses.translation_dramatic: They came close, the wicked, mouths open, ready to eat me alive: my adversaries, my enemies, every one of them set against me. And they stumbled. They stumbled, and they fell.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene is a pack closing in. 'To eat my flesh' is the language of predators, and probably of slander too, but the text does not say which; Radak and Meiri hear it as a literal threat, Malbim splits it into motives of greed and of hatred. Let the actors close in slowly, then give the last two verbs, 'stumbled and fell', as a small silence: the enemy does the falling.

The KJV, ASV and Webster all render the verb 'came upon' and make the sentence past ("came upon me"); the Hebrew is an infinitive with a preposition, 'in the drawing near of', which leaves it open whether this is memory or promise (Radak sees it as remembered experience: 'I saw that it happened many times'). The KJV also moves 'wicked' before 'even mine enemies', turning a list of three words (evildoers, adversaries, enemies) into one. The BBE 'put an end to me' loses the eating image altogether.

philological_notes.note: 'To eat my flesh': a predator image. Meiri and Radak read it as the threat to kill; Malbim distinguishes thieves who devour for gain from enemies who attack for hatred.
Stumbled and fell: the verbs are in the perfect, a completed event, and the hendiadys marks a total, unforced collapse. Malbim: they fall by their own counsel, without my acting.

verses.translation_literal: If a camp encamps against me, my heart will not fear; if war rises against me, in this I [am] trusting.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let an army pitch its tents around me, and my heart will not shake. Let war itself stand up against me: even then, in this, I am secure.
verses.directors_commentary:
From memory the singer moves to hypothesis: 'if', not 'when'. The Hebrew plays on the root חנה twice in three words, 'a camp encamps' (תַּחֲנֶה מַחֲנֶה), and no English 'host should encamp' (KJV) keeps the sound. 'Camp' is a mobile army town of tents; a force that camps against you has settled in for a siege, not a raid. The heart is the seat of mind and will, not feeling only: Radak says 'my heart and my understanding is what makes me trust'.

The KJV 'in this will I be confident' hides a real ambiguity in בְּזֹאת, 'in this'. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David take it back to v. 1, 'YHWH is my light'; Ibn Ezra reports others who point forward to the one request of v. 4. The verb בטח means to rest your weight on something, not to feel 'confident'; the participle makes it a continuing posture rather than a vow.

philological_notes.note: Verb and noun from the same root: 'a camp camps'. The verb is feminine to agree with 'camp'; Meiri notes the noun is treated as feminine here, as in Gen 32:9 ('the one camp').
'In this': refers either back to 'YHWH is my light and salvation and stronghold' or forward to the request of v. 4.
Participle: 'trusting', a settled state, not a one-time decision.

verses.translation_literal: One [thing] I have asked from beside YHWH, it I will seek: my dwelling in the house of YHWH all the days of my life, to look on the kindness of YHWH and to inquire in his temple.
verses.translation_dramatic: One thing I have asked of the LORD. Only one, and it I will keep seeking: to live in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze on the LORD in his sweetness, and to ask my questions in his temple.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone changes. After three verses of defiance the singer narrows to a single wish, and the wish is a place, not a victory. Say 'one' as if everything else were being set down on the floor. The verbs are in two tenses on purpose: 'I have asked' (done) and 'I will seek' (still doing), so the desire is old and not yet satisfied.

'The house of the LORD' and 'his temple' (הֵיכָל, a word borrowed from the palace, 'great house') place the singer at a sanctuary; Radak says the house where the ark was, with its prophets, priests and Levites, and Ibn Ezra dates the psalm to David's old age. To live in it 'all the days of my life' is not a priest's job but a longing, and the KJV 'dwell' is fair. The KJV 'beauty' for נֹעַם is a stretch: the word means pleasantness, kindness, the sweetness of a person's company, and Metzudat David reads it as the pleasantness of the Lord's teaching. The KJV also moves 'desired' in for 'asked' (שָׁאַל, to ask, as one asks a favour).

The last verb, לְבַקֵּר, splits the commentators: 'inquire' with Lev 27:33 (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion), 'visit every morning' (Rashi's Dunash; a play on בֹּקֶר, morning), or consult the priests. 'Inquire' keeps the oracular sense, asking a question of God in his house.

philological_notes.note: 'To look on': the verb of the seer and the prophetic vision, not the ordinary 'to see'. Ibn Ezra hears it as the unveiling of the secrets of creation.
Pleasantness, kindness, graciousness: said of a person whose company is sweet. 'Beauty' (KJV) is possible but narrower. Metzudat David reads 'the pleasantness of the Lord's Torah'.
Disputed. Either 'to inquire / to examine' (as in Lev 27:33, 'he shall not inquire between good and bad'), or 'to go each morning'. The consonants allow both.

verses.translation_literal: For he will treasure me in a booth in a day of evil; he will hide me in the hiding-place of his tent; on a rock he will lift me up.
verses.translation_dramatic: For when the evil day comes, he will take me in and keep me, as a treasure is kept, under his own shelter. He will hide me in the secret place of his tent, where no eye follows. And then he will lift me out of reach, high on a rock.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this verse as a man who is already inside. He is not asking for protection; he is describing the room he is standing in. Three images, one after another: a booth, a tent, a rock. A booth (sukkah-like, a covering of branches) is what a farmer or shepherd throws up for shade, a temporary, humble thing; the tent is the sanctuary, the one place where the king's own enemies cannot walk in. Ibn Ezra takes the booth to be Jerusalem, citing 'in Salem is his booth' (Ps 76:3), and Rashi, quoting Seder Olam, takes the verse to be about Joash, hidden for six years in the temple by his aunt (2 Kings 11:3). Both are readings of a text that never names the place.

The verb 'hide' is said twice with two different roots: צפן in the first line, סתר in the second. The first root is the word for storing something precious (so, a treasure that is kept out of sight); this is my own reading of the root, not a claim of the commentators. The KJV renders both with 'hide', which flattens the first into mere concealment, and it turns the booth into a 'pavilion' (a word that suggests a royal canopy, which the Hebrew does not) and the tent into a 'tabernacle', which carries Old Testament and New Testament freight that the Hebrew 'ohel' (plain tent) does not. 'Day of evil' (yom ra'ah) is the Hebrew idiom for a day of calamity; the KJV's 'time of trouble' softens evil into trouble. Ibn Ezra even takes it as an astrological 'evil configuration' of the stars against one's fate, which gives some sense of how ominous the phrase was.

The Targum does not keep the booth as a booth: it renders it as 'in his shade/shelter' (בְּטַלְלֵיהּ) and keeps a verb of hiding in both lines. 'On a rock' is the final lift: Rashi glosses it with Ps 40:3 ('he set my feet on a rock'), Metzudat David with the soldier who stands above and so overcomes the one below. Think of a high crag in the Judean wilderness: height is safety.

philological_notes.note: 'He will store me up, treasure me': the root means to hide away something valuable, to keep a thing in store. It is stronger than a plain 'conceal' and is paired in the next line with a different root for hiding (סתר).
A booth or covert, from the root 'to cover'. The final ה is an old spelling of the suffix 'his' (STEPBible lemma סֹךְ). Ibn Ezra identifies it with Jerusalem (comparing Ps 76:3).
'In the hiding-place of his tent': the innermost part of the sanctuary tent. Rashi, citing Seder Olam, ties it to the room in the temple where Joash was hidden.

verses.translation_literal: And now my head will be lifted up above my enemies round about me, and I will sacrifice in his tent sacrifices of a shout; I will sing and I will make music to YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now, my head will rise above the enemies who ring me round. And in his tent I will bring sacrifices with a great shout. I will sing. I will make music for the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image completes itself: the man set on the rock now lifts his head, the posture of someone who has stopped being afraid (compare 'lifted up' in v. 5, the same root רום). Play 'and now' as the turn from petition to victory, though the singer has not yet won anything; Ibn Ezra says the head is raised even if there is no more fighting, because it is in the hiding place of the Most High.

The KJV adds 'therefore', which the Hebrew does not have: the promise of sacrifice is joined by 'and', not by a conclusion. 'Sacrifices of joy' in the KJV softens תְּרוּעָה, which is a shout, a battle-cry or a trumpet-blast; Malbim notes that the same word is used for war trumpets (Num 10:9), so the sacrifice is the thank-offering for a victory. Rashi hears 'sacrifices over which a song is said'. 'Sing' and 'make music' are two verbs of different sort: שִׁיר is the voice, זָמַר is music with instruments, so the singer promises voice and strings both.

philological_notes.note: A shout: of joy, of alarm, of battle or of trumpets. 'Sacrifices of a shout' is a thanksgiving offering accompanied by acclamation.
Two cohortative verbs: the first is singing, the second is making music or praise-song.

verses.translation_literal: Hear, YHWH, my voice: I call; and be gracious to me and answer me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear me, LORD. Hear my voice. I am calling. Be kind to me. Answer me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Everything changes at this verse, in tone and in grammar: the confidence of vv. 1–6 drops away and the singer is on his knees, speaking short imperatives in the second person. Many modern readers think a second poem begins here. Whatever the origin, the actors should hear the contrast: the long, rolling lines of trust give way to four clipped commands, and the voice is a real voice, out loud.

The KJV 'when I cry with my voice' supplies a conjunction that the Hebrew lacks; the two clauses stand side by side, 'hear my voice — I call'. Ibn Ezra notes the missing אשר. The KJV 'have mercy also upon me' puts in an 'also' where the Hebrew has only 'and'; חָנֵּנִי means 'show me favour', the answer owed to someone who asks without a claim. ענני is the formal word for a reply, as to a petition.

philological_notes.note: 'Be gracious to me': from חנן, to show unearned favour. The same root gives 'grace' in other contexts; mercy (KJV) is a fair but narrower rendering.
Imperfect, 'I call' or 'I am calling'. Ibn Ezra reads the clause as having a dropped relative 'which'.

verses.translation_literal: To you my heart has said, 'Seek my face'; your face, YHWH, I will seek.
verses.translation_dramatic: My heart has spoken for you. It has said, 'Seek my face.' And I answer it, with all I am: your face, LORD, your face is what I will seek.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is one of the hardest verses in the Psalms to speak, because the Hebrew has no 'when' and no 'God said'. It has a heart that speaks, and the line 'Seek my face' hangs without a clear speaker. Is it the heart, repeating what it senses is God's call? Is it God, speaking to the heart? Is it the speaker, calling the whole people to seek him? The actor must pick, and the picking changes the scene. I would play it simply: the heart speaks, and the man answers it by obeying.

The verse is built on a mirror: 'seek my face' and then 'your face I will seek', with the same word for face in the plural, and the same verb, first as a command (plural, to a whole company) and then as a promise (singular, 'I'). The quotation is the voice of the heart; the second half is the man's own voice, accepting. The word 'face' matters in the ancient world: to seek someone's face is to ask for an audience, to come into the presence, and it is the court language of a petitioner before a king.

The small word לְךָ 'to you / for you' is the real puzzle. Rashi reads it as 'on your errand, in your place': the heart speaks as your messenger, telling all of Israel to seek the divine face, and he obeys it (he compares Job 33:6 and 13:8 for the same idiom). Ibn Ezra reads it as 'for your sake'. Meiri reads it the same way, 'for your honour', and adds that other commentators 'struggled much with it'. The KJV takes the lines as a address in which God speaks ('When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee'): it adds a 'when', and it makes God the speaker of the first command. YLT is closer to the Hebrew in leaving the heart as the speaker.

philological_notes.note: 'To you my heart has said' or 'for you my heart has said'. The preposition is read as 'on your behalf' by Rashi and Meiri, and as 'for your sake' by Ibn Ezra. The verb is third-person masculine singular, with 'heart' as the subject: the heart is the speaker.
Plural imperative, 'seek (all of you) my face'. The quotation is plural while the answer is singular, which is why Rashi reads the call as addressed to all Israel.

verses.translation_literal: Do not hide your face from me; do not turn aside your servant in anger. My help you have been; do not abandon me and do not forsake me, God of my salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not hide your face from me. Do not turn your servant away in anger. You have been my help. Do not cast me off, do not leave me, God who saves me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer turns from asking to begging, and the verbs pile up in the negative: do not hide, do not turn aside, do not abandon, do not forsake. Hiding the face is the ancient picture of a deity's withdrawn favour, the opposite of the 'face' sought in v. 8; the singer has just promised to seek that face, so its absence is the worst case. The one positive sentence, 'my help you have been', sits like a plank in the middle: it is the argument, 'you have already done it'.

The KJV 'Hide not thy face far from me' adds a 'far' that the Hebrew does not have, and 'put not thy servant away' is a paraphrase of תַּט־בְּאַף, 'turn aside in anger'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take the verb as transitive, 'do not make your servant turn/bend aside'; Radak reads it as 'do not distract me with the world's affairs, which are anger and trouble'. The two verbs at the end, נָטַשׁ and עָזַב, are near-synonyms (Metzudat Zion says one repeats the other with different words), and the KJV's 'leave... forsake' keeps both. 'My help' (עֶזְרָתִי) is a title God holds in the Psalms; the singer is invoking it.

philological_notes.note: 'Do not turn aside in anger': Rashi compares 'he bowed the heavens' (Ps 18:10); Ibn Ezra takes עבדך as the object, as in 'a leaning wall'. KJV 'put away' is an interpretation.
Two verbs for abandoning, in parallel. Metzudat Zion: 'he repeats the thing in other words.' The second verb returns in v. 10.

verses.translation_literal: For my father and my mother have forsaken me, and YHWH will gather me in.
verses.translation_dramatic: My father and my mother have left me. But the LORD will gather me in.
verses.directors_commentary:
The most intimate line in the chapter, and the shortest. In a world with no state welfare, an abandoned child belongs to nobody: the family is the only safety, and the orphan, widow and stranger are the people God is said to defend. To be 'gathered' (אָסַף) is to be taken into a household, as one gathers in a stray animal or an unprotected person (Malbim: an orphan whom God takes into his house to raise).

The KJV 'When my father and my mother forsake me, then...' turns a statement into a hypothesis, and puts in the 'then' that the Hebrew lacks. The Hebrew כִּי with a perfect verb gives a flat fact, 'my father and mother have forsaken me', and then a future, 'and YHWH will gather me'. Ibn Ezra reads it as a certainty; Meiri and Radak read it as 'when I left my parents' home, you took me in'. Most modern readers hear a literal or figurative orphan. Rashi's rabbinic homily about the begetting is a different reading and should not be played. The verb is the same one used in v. 9 (עזב), so the singer's 'do not forsake me' is answered by a parent's own forsaking.

philological_notes.note: The same root as 'do not forsake me' in v. 9: the singer's fear is already, in the family, a fact.
To gather, receive, take in, as in gathering the harvest or the stray, or being gathered to one's people at death. Metzudat David: he gathers me by giving all my lack.

verses.translation_literal: Teach me, YHWH, your way, and lead me in a path of level ground, on account of my watchers.
verses.translation_dramatic: Teach me your way, LORD. Lead me on a level path, because of those who are watching me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two requests: be taught, and be led. The 'way' (דֶּרֶךְ) is the road God walks and the conduct he asks, and a 'path of level ground' (אֹרַח מִישׁוֹר) is a road with no rocks to trip on: a clear route, in the moral sense too. Ibn Ezra quotes a sage: the man who wants to overcome his enemies should add to his service of God. The reason clause is the key to the playing: the singer asks to walk straight because he is watched.

The KJV 'because of mine enemies' is a translation of the word's context, not of the word. שׁוֹרְרַי comes from שׁוּר, to look, watch or lie in wait, so these are 'watchers', people who study him for a slip; Metzudat Zion links it with 'my watchers have gnashed' (Ps 56:3), and Radak compares Saul eyeing David (1 Sam 18:9). YLT's 'my beholders' is closer than the KJV. Metzudat David: if I stumble in God's ways and am punished, my watchers will rejoice. The KJV 'plain path' is serviceable; 'plain' here means flat, not simple.

philological_notes.note: 'My watchers': those who look on with ill will, lying in wait. Metzudat Zion ties it to Ps 56:3; Radak to 1 Sam 18:9 (Saul 'eyed' David).
A path of level or straight ground; both 'smooth' and 'upright' are in the word.

verses.translation_literal: Do not give me over to the throat of my adversaries, for witnesses of falsehood have risen against me, and one breathing out violence.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not hand me over to the hunger of my enemies. False witnesses have stood up against me, and one who breathes violence with every breath.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a courtroom, not a battlefield. 'Witnesses of falsehood' are men who swear false evidence, and in a legal system run by testimony in the gate there is no other proof; an accusation backed by two voices could kill (Deut 19:15–21, not in the packet). Radak imagines them saying 'he is wicked and a man of blood and has no share in the LORD'. Play the last words as menace, the voice of a man who talks hatred.

The KJV 'will of mine enemies' is an accurate guess, and every commentator agrees (Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion: 'in the desire of'), but the Hebrew word is נֶפֶשׁ, which means 'throat' and so 'appetite': the singer is not to be given to their appetite, and that echoes the 'eating of flesh' in v. 2. The KJV 'such as breathe out cruelty' keeps the participle but hides the form: וִיפֵחַ is a noun ('a puffer-out of violence', Ibn Ezra: one who speaks), so there is a second witness who is a whole person made of violent breath. Note the STEPBible gloss 'a witness of' for this word is borrowed from the first half and has no lexical support. The dramatic breath is the point: violence is said, not done, in this verse.

philological_notes.note: 'In the nephesh of my foes': nephesh is throat, appetite, will. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all read it as 'desire, will'; Radak compares Gen 23:8 'if it is your nephesh'.
False witnesses. Radak and Meiri: they testify that David is wicked and a man of blood.
'One breathing out violence': a form from the root 'to puff, breathe out'. Rashi: speakers of evil; Metzudat Zion: speech that comes with a breath of the mouth; Meiri compares Hab 2:3.

verses.translation_literal: If not — I had believed — to see the goodness of YHWH in the land of the living.
verses.translation_dramatic: Had I not believed… had I not held on to the belief that I would yet see the goodness of the LORD, here, in the land of the living.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a sentence that breaks off in mid-breath. The Hebrew opens with לוּלֵא, 'if not', and never says what would have happened. The KJV (and the ASV and Webster) fill the silence with 'I had fainted', in italics in the original printing; the Hebrew has no such verb. The gap is the point: the speaker cannot finish the sentence because the alternative is unthinkable. Play it as a man who stops, swallows and turns to what he did hold on to. Every commentator fills the gap differently: Radak and Rashi have the false witnesses of verse 12 destroying him, Ibn Ezra has the enemies almost ruling over him.

In the Masoretic text this word is marked with dots above its letters, the so-called puncta extraordinaria, which the Talmud (b. Berakhot 4a, cited by Rashi and Radak) takes as David's doubt: he knew God pays the righteous in the world to come but did not know whether sin had cost him a share. The KJV 'to see the goodness of the Lord' is accurate, but its 'land of the living' reads as a pious idiom. For an ancient hearer the contrast is with Sheol, the land of the dead: to 'see' means to experience, and 'the land of the living' is simply this life, where a man can still be rescued. Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion read it so; Radak and Meiri read it as the world to come, the garden of Eden. The Hebrew allows both and the actor need not choose.

philological_notes.note: 'If not', 'were it not that'. It introduces a condition whose result is unstated, so the verse is an unfinished sentence. In the Masoretic text it is dotted (puncta extraordinaria), and the Talmud reads the dots as a mark of David's doubt.
'In the land of the living': the world of those who are alive, set against Sheol. Whether it means this world or the world to come is disputed among the classical commentators.

token_glosses.gloss: if not, were it not that

verses.translation_literal: Wait for YHWH; be strong, and let your heart be firm; and wait for YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Wait for the LORD. Be strong, and let your heart hold firm. And wait. Wait for the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the last line of the psalm and its last command. The speaker turns, and it is no longer God who is addressed but himself, or the listener in the room: Radak hears a man saying it to his own soul all day long; Metzudat David, 'I said to my soul, hope in the LORD'. The one who asks for help in verses 7 to 12 ends by giving the instruction that held him up. Say it low, like a person who has been talking to himself for a long time.

The verb is the same at the start and at the end: 'wait' (qavveh), a word for waiting that carries the sense of hoping, of leaning forward in expectation. It is not sitting idle; it is the stance of someone who is sure that the answer is coming. The frame of the repetition is the point. Metzudat David says it is doubled 'for its continuity', and Radak says the hope should be there always and never leave the heart. Malbim goes further: hope in people is a means to an end, and the end is to stop hoping once one has what one wanted; but hope in the LORD is its own end, a state worth having for itself.

The middle phrase has a small grammar puzzle. 'Be strong' is an imperative, but 'let your heart be firm' (veya'ametz libbekha) is a different mood, a jussive of the causative stem. Ibn Ezra reads the verb as transitive: 'he (the LORD) will make your heart firm'. That is how the KJV renders it ('he shall strengthen thine heart'), where the Hebrew leaves the subject open. The KJV also pads the last clause with 'I say', which is not in the Hebrew: the repetition is the emphasis, not a speaker's aside. 'Be of good courage' is a Victorian softening of 'be strong', the same word used to command soldiers.

philological_notes.note: 'Wait, hope': a verb of expectant waiting, used twice, at the beginning and end of the verse. Malbim says that hope in the LORD is an end in itself, unlike hope in a person, whose aim is to stop hoping once the thing is received; Radak says the repetition means the hope must never leave the heart.
A jussive, 'and let it be firm / may he strengthen'. Ibn Ezra reads it as transitive, so that the LORD is the one who strengthens the heart; Metzudat Zion glosses the root as 'strength and firmness'.
